headlines.summary: Follow Apple’s Sept. 9 event live for new product announcements, prices, release dates and the company’s first launch under CEO John Ternus.
headlines.article_text: Apple event today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu watch now VIDEO 3:36 03:36 Apple is expected to unveil its first-ever foldable iPhone: Here's what you need to know TechCheck Apple will kick off its biggest launch event of the year on Wednesday, Sept. 9, at 10 a.m. PT / 1 p.m. ET. Viewers can watch the event, which carries the tagline "Surprise and shine," on Apple's website . While Apple hasn't officially said what it will introduce, analysts expect new iPhone models, including the company's first folding phone, as well as new Apple Watches. Investors are also closely watching to see if Apple raises starting prices for its iPhones during a global computer parts shortage. The company raised prices on Macs and iPads over the summer. It's the debut event for Apple CEO John Ternus , who took the helm on Sept. 1. The longtime hardware engineer will appear at an Apple keynote for the first time as CEO, and Apple customers and investors are watching to see where he follows in Tim Cook's footsteps, and where he diverges. The event could also focus on artificial intelligence, as Apple is expected to release its new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence software to the public alongside the new hardware in the coming days. Read more CNBC news on Apple Xiaomi, Huawei take on Apple's rumored foldable iPhone Apple shares are doing something they haven't done in 20 years Apple enters John Ternus era as AI challenges and memory crunch intensify 5 Min Ago What consumers can expect to pay watch now VIDEO 1:55 01:55 Apple could unveil its first foldable iPhone in major premium push Squawk Box Asia Apple's prices are in focus after Cook said increases were "unavoidable" during a global shortage of computer parts, especially memory. Folding phones are also more expensive than typical phones because of the increased cost for the folding screen and the hinge. Samsung's Z Fold 8 retails for $1,900. Analysts say Apple's customers are affluent and may be willing to pay even more for the company's biggest iPhone redesign in nearly a decade. Market researcher IDC says it expects an Apple folding phone to cost $2,500 or more. Meanwhile, JPMorgan Chase analysts see Apple's foldable costing at least $1,999 when it comes out. At those prices, the phone would cost more than many of Apple's laptops. Analysts widely believe that would lead to lower sales volumes than for Apple's traditional iPhones. "The widely anticipated launch of the foldable iPhone will be less influential on unit outcomes, but more so drive investor confidence in the company's ability to stand up and deliver success with a new premium device," JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee wrote earlier this month. — Kif Leswing 36 Min Ago Investors are skittish headed into event Apple's stock over the past five days Apple shares slipped on Wednesday, dropping for a third straight day and fourth in five, as investors prepared to be underwhelmed. Analysts at KeyBanc Capital Markets wrote in a note last week that the launch event is "likely a negative catalyst for shares," because a large increase in prices would hurt volume sales while a minimal change would amplify the "focus on gross margins." The firm is one of the very few tracked by FactSet with a sell rating on Apple. The stock is still up 15% for the year, slightly outperforming the Nasdaq. — Ari Levy 1 Hour Ago When can we expect iPhones to hit store shelves? People shop at an Apple store in lower Manhattan on July 30, 2026 in New York City. Spencer Platt | Getty Images Based on past launch dates, Apple's new iPhone typically hits store shelves on the Friday that comes the week after the keynote. This year, that would be Sept. 18. Apple typically opens preorders on its website and at retail partners about a week before that. — Kif Leswing 2 Hours Ago Video: Can Apple capitalize on a major upgrade cycle with AI and personal agents? watch now VIDEO 4:56 04:56 Apple set to unveil iPhone 18: What the release means for the tech giant Squawk Box 2 Hours Ago Ternus makes his second-ever X post John Ternus, senior vice president of hardware engineering at Apple Inc., during an Apple event in New York, US, on Wednesday, March 4, 2026. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty Images Ternus took to X on Wednesday morning to make his second-ever post to the platform . The new Apple CEO shared a vague, 14-second video showing a light shining on, well. something. His first post, made on Sept. 1, said "hello." —Chris Eudaily 3 Hours Ago Apple's rivals are watching closely Apple's fiercest rivals for smartphone sales in China are reacting to the launch, even before it's started, CNBC reported this week. Huawei and Xiaomi both announced new foldable phones on Tuesday. Xiaomi introduced the 18 Fold, a passport-sized device, and Huawei unveiled the Mate XT2, a trifold smartphone. The new Xiaomi 18 Fold smartphone is displayed at a specialty store on September 8, 2026 in Zhengzhou, Henan Province of China. Visual China Group | Getty Images Foldable phones remain a very small part of the overall smartphone market, or about 2.2% of unit shipments so far this year, according to IDC. Huawei is currently the dominant player, especially in China, where it controls nearly 80% of the market. But Apple's potential debut is expected to energize the entire category. — Kif Leswing

headlines.article_text: CoreWeave CEO says speed of AI change is 'frightening' the public Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator said he thinks artificial intelligence companies haven't explained the technology's benefits well enough to the public. Those comments came during the Goldman Sachs' Communcacopia + Technology conference, which brings together leaders across the biggest tech and media companies. watch now VIDEO 4:22 04:22 CoreWeave CEO: AI industry has not done a good job explaining data center impact on communities Squawk on the Street The public opposition to artificial intelligence and data centers is front and center at the Goldman Sachs Communcacopia + Technology Conference. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator told CNBC's David Faber that companies haven't explained the technology's benefits well enough to the public. "I don't think we have done a particularly good job of talking about the benefits of what the data centers allow the AI companies to be able to deliver to people, to governments, to decision making," Intrator said in comments that aired Wednesday. The annual conference brings together leaders across the biggest tech and media companies, and AI adoption — along with the pushback many local communities are showing towards its buildout — is perhaps one of the biggest opportunities, and risks, facing businesses of every kind. Intrator insisted that the fear around the transformation isn't about data centers, specifically, but is about how fast things are changing. "It is really about: Hey, you know the world is changing, and it's changing very quickly, and that's going to have impacts on myself. It's going to have impacts on my children, and what is that going to look like? And that is frightening," he added. As Goldman's conference got underway, another set of comments in the tech world caught attention as an AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic Tuesday, warning the rapidly-evolving technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade." Jacob Coxon, who worked at both Anthropic and its chief competitor OpenAI, accused the companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race towards AI superintelligence. "Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing," Coxon wrote in a post on X announcing his resignation.
